opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think Energy Star is a really useful model to look at, partly because it's so simple from the consumer's point of view. When you go buy a fridge or a dishwasher, you don't need to understand compressor efficiency or kilowatt-hours per cycle. You see a label, and it tells you, relative to other products in that category, whether this one is more or less efficient. That relative comparison within a category is the key idea, and I think it maps really well onto AI.

With AI models, people are often choosing between models that do the same task: text generation, image generation, summarization, classification. Right now there's basically no way for them to know that one model might use ten or a hundred times more energy than another to do roughly the same thing. So the first lesson from Energy Star is to compare like with like. You don't compare a fridge to a washing machine, and you shouldn't compare an image generation model to a sentiment classifier. You define tasks, run models on standardized datasets and hardware, measure the energy for inference, and then rate them on a relative scale, like one to five stars.

The second lesson is standardization and transparency in how you measure. Energy Star works because there's an agreed-upon testing protocol. For AI, that means controlling for the hardware, the batch size, the number of queries, and so on, so the numbers are actually comparable and reproducible. Otherwise everyone reports whatever flatters them.

The third lesson is that the bar has to move over time. Energy Star periodically updates its thresholds as technology improves, so a five-star appliance from fifteen years ago wouldn't necessarily be five stars today. AI is moving incredibly fast, so ratings need to be recalibrated regularly as new, more efficient models come out.

Where AI differs is that a lot of the most widely used models are closed. You can't just take them into a lab and test them the way you can an appliance. So part of the challenge is getting companies to participate, either by submitting their models for testing or by disclosing numbers under a common methodology. I think a voluntary, well-designed rating can create positive pressure. Once there's a label that users, developers, and procurement people care about, nobody wants to be the one-star model. Eventually you could imagine regulators referencing this kind of standard too.

Ultimately, the goal is the same as Energy Star's: make energy efficiency a visible factor in decision-making. Right now it's invisible, and invisible costs don't get optimized. If we give people a simple, trustworthy signal, they can choose the smaller, more efficient model when it's good enough for the job, and in a lot of cases it really is.

r001.rationale: The response proposes comparing models that perform the same task and rating their inference energy on a relative scale.

r002.rationale: It discusses standardized testing controls but does not identify the EPA’s use of a default operating setting.

r003.rationale: It discusses measuring energy and choosing a model that is good enough, but does not clearly distinguish energy-efficiency measurement from task-performance evaluation.

r004.rationale: It mentions controlling hardware, batch size, and query count, but does not state that model performance depends on how the model is used.

r005.rationale: It proposes a relative one-to-five-star scale within task categories, but does not say rating categories should be derived from each task’s measured efficiency range.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Energy Star is actually the thing that got me thinking about this in the first place. When you go buy a fridge or a washing machine, you don't have to be an electrical engineer to make a decision. There's a little label, it tells you roughly how much energy the thing uses per year, and there's this star or letter grade that lets you compare it to other appliances in the same category. And what I think is really powerful about that is it's category-specific. Nobody is comparing a fridge to a lightbulb. You compare fridges to fridges.

And that's exactly the piece that's missing with AI right now. People will say "this model is efficient" or "this model is huge," but efficient compared to what? A tiny classification model and a big generative model aren't doing the same task, so putting them on the same scale doesn't tell you anything. So the way we approached it, with the AI Energy Score project, was to say, okay, let's define tasks: text generation, image generation, summarization, speech, whatever. Within each task, you run every model on the same hardware, with the same standardized set of inputs, you measure the energy with the actual power draw on the GPU, and then you rate models relative to each other within that task. Five stars means you're among the most efficient for that task, one star means you're among the least. It's a relative scale, and that's intentional, because the field moves so fast that an absolute threshold would be meaningless within six months.

The other thing I borrowed from Energy Star is the idea that the label has to be simple enough to actually influence behavior. We publish all the raw numbers for people who want them, but the star rating is what you'd put on a model card, or what a company procuring a model would look at. The goal is to create a market signal. Right now there's basically no incentive for developers to make models more efficient, because nobody can see it. If efficiency becomes visible and comparable, then it becomes something you can compete on.

Where the analogy breaks down a bit is that an appliance is a physical thing with fixed hardware, and a model's energy use depends enormously on how it's deployed: what GPUs, what batch size, what quantization, where the data center is. So we had to make a lot of choices to standardize that away, and we're very upfront that this is a benchmark, not a measurement of real-world footprint. And the other hard part is that Energy Star works partly because manufacturers are required, or strongly nudged, to participate. With AI, we can test open models ourselves, but for closed models, we need the companies to run the benchmark and report, and so far participation has been pretty uneven. That's really the next frontier: not the methodology, but getting it to the point where disclosure is expected, the way it is for your dishwasher.

r001.rationale: The response says models should be compared within each defined task, using the same hardware and standardized inputs.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the EPA or a default operating setting for standardizing appliance measurements.

r003.rationale: It discusses energy measurement and task categories, but does not distinguish measuring energy efficiency from evaluating task performance.

r004.rationale: It says energy use depends on deployment choices; it does not state that model performance depends on how the model is used.

r005.rationale: It proposes relative star ratings within each task, assigning higher and lower ratings based on which models are most and least efficient.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful thing about Energy Star is that you don’t have to understand how a refrigerator works to compare it with another refrigerator. There’s a standardized way of measuring energy consumption, and that information is available when you’re making a decision. We need something similar for AI.

But we have to compare models doing comparable tasks, under comparable conditions. What does it cost in energy to answer a question, classify a document, or generate an image? And what quality are you getting for that energy? A single rating that mixes all those uses together wouldn’t be particularly helpful.

I’d also want to distinguish the energy used to train a model from the energy used to run it. Training is an upfront cost, whereas inference happens every time someone uses the model. Having that information in an accessible label would help people choose a model that meets their needs without assuming that the biggest model is always the best choice.

r001.rationale: It says models should be compared when they perform comparable tasks under comparable conditions.

r002.rationale: It mentions standardized energy measurement but does not identify the EPA’s default operating setting.

r003.rationale: It considers energy use alongside the quality obtained, distinguishing energy measurement from task performance.

r004.rationale: It explains that useful comparisons depend on the task, with different examples such as answering questions, classifying documents, and generating images.

r005.rationale: It rejects a single rating across uses but does not propose deriving rating categories from measured efficiency ranges within each task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful thing about Energy Star is that you don’t have to be an expert in how a refrigerator works to compare it with another refrigerator. There’s a standardized measurement, and that gives you something concrete to base your decision on. We need something similar for AI models.

But we have to be clear about what we’re comparing. A model that generates images and a model that classifies text are doing different jobs. So I’d want ratings based on a particular task, measured under consistent conditions, with the model’s performance alongside its energy use. Then you can ask: for the level of accuracy I need, which model uses the least energy?

And energy isn’t exactly the same as carbon emissions, because that also depends on where the electricity comes from. An energy-efficiency label would be a useful starting point, but we should make those distinctions visible. The goal is to help people make informed choices without requiring them to run all these measurements themselves.

r001.rationale: It proposes ratings for a particular task under consistent conditions and compares energy use for the needed performance level.

r002.rationale: It mentions standardized measurement but does not identify the EPA’s default operating setting.

r003.rationale: It treats task performance and energy use as separate measures to consider together in an efficiency rating.

r004.rationale: It notes that models do different jobs, but does not say a model’s performance depends on how it is used.

r005.rationale: It proposes task-based ratings but does not derive rating categories from the measured efficiency range.
